title: Punctuation Marks and the Meanings They Carry

blocks.text: "The teacher said the prefect is late." "The teacher, said the prefect, is late." Two commas, and the accusation changes hands completely. Punctuation is not decoration added after the words; it is part of the grammar, and it decides who did what.

blocks.markdown:
Punctuation does three jobs:

1. It shows where sentences **begin and end**.
2. It shows how the parts inside a sentence **relate** to one another.
3. It removes **ambiguity** so the reader takes only the meaning you intended.

In the WAEC essay paper, punctuation is assessed under Mechanical Accuracy alongside spelling and grammar, so careless marks cost marks.

rows: We bought yams, rice and beans.
She packed carefully; the journey was long.
Bring three things: a pen, a ruler and a card.
Encloses an aside or adds an afterthought
The library — newly built — was opened.
blocks.caption: The punctuation marks required at senior secondary level

blocks.title: Semicolon or colon?
blocks.text: A **semicolon** balances: what follows is another complete statement of equal weight. A **colon** points forward: what follows explains, itemises or completes what came before. If you can replace the mark with a full stop, a semicolon is possible. If you can replace it with the word *namely*, a colon is right.

blocks.markdown:
### Commas that change meaning

**Defining clause — no commas.** The clause picks out which one you mean:
> The candidates **who arrived late** were turned away. (only the late ones)

**Non-defining clause — commas.** The clause merely adds information:
> My brother, **who lives in Kano**, is a pharmacist. (I have one brother)

Removing the commas from the second sentence would imply that you have several brothers and are identifying one of them. This distinction is a favourite examination item.

blocks.title: Repairing a badly punctuated sentence
blocks.prompt: Correct the punctuation: "The rain started early, however, the match went ahead."

steps.text: Find the finite verbs: *started* and *went*. Two verbs mean two clauses.
Test whether each clause could stand alone. 'The rain started early' and 'the match went ahead' both can, so both are main clauses.
Check the joining word. *However* is a conjunctive adverb, not a coordinating conjunction, so it cannot join two main clauses with only a comma before it.
Apply the rule: a conjunctive adverb needs a semicolon or a full stop in front of it, and a comma after it.
Write the corrected version: 'The rain started early; however, the match went ahead.'
Note the alternatives: 'The rain started early. However, the match went ahead.' or, using a real conjunction, 'The rain started early, but the match went ahead.'

blocks.answer: The rain started early; however, the match went ahead.

items: Punctuation belonging to the spoken words goes **inside** the quotation marks: "Where are the scripts?" asked the invigilator.
The reporting phrase after a quotation stays in **lower case**: "Come in," she said.
Never put a comma between a verb and its object: *We bought yams* — not *We bought, yams*.
*However*, *therefore*, *moreover* and *nevertheless* need a semicolon or full stop before them, not a comma.
Use a pair of dashes or a pair of brackets, never one of each.

blocks.title: The comma splice
blocks.text: Joining two main clauses with only a comma — "The bus was full, we waited for the next one" — is one of the most heavily penalised errors in the essay paper. Fix it with a conjunction, a semicolon or a full stop.

blocks.title: WAEC and NECO tip
blocks.text: When you finish an essay, reread it looking only at the punctuation. Check every comma to see whether it is separating list items, enclosing an aside or wrongly splicing two sentences. Two minutes of this saves several Mechanical Accuracy marks.

points: Punctuation marks sentence boundaries, shows internal relationships and removes ambiguity.
A semicolon joins two independent clauses; a colon introduces a list or explanation.
Commas round a relative clause make it non-defining; no commas make it defining.
Punctuation belonging to spoken words goes inside the quotation marks.
*However* and similar adverbs need a semicolon or full stop before them.
Joining two main clauses with a comma alone is a comma splice and always an error.
